rationale: A wins because it gives the founder real editorial risk, not just tidy pitch lanes: "What 40 chain optometry clinics mean for the independent eye doctor down the street" is the uncomfortable protagonist choice a reporter can actually sell. B is competent, but "Warby Parker is testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" overclaims a pilot with no results and turns a channel question into a made-up bakeoff. A also has the sharper discipline: "an anonymous pilot is a press release, not a story" is exactly the judgment this exercise needed.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker's new stores are optometry clinics that happen to sell frames" overstates the supplied fact. The update says most new stores will offer optometrist-staffed exams, not that the stores are primarily clinics.
"Warby was the canonical case study for that thesis" leans on outside reputation not supplied in the fact block. Useful, but not cleanly grounded.

"retail chains are absorbing routine eye care" broadens one Warby expansion into a sector-wide shift without market evidence. The set wisely asks for proof, but the angle still walks close to thesis-first framing.
gaps_in_B: "a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" invents a performance comparison. The fact is only that Warby is piloting sales through a national pharmacy chain.
"LensCrafters, Costco Optical" are named competitors not present in the update. That may be reasonable background, but under this blind fact set it is decoration, not grounding.
"the CVS-MinuteClinic-style trend" imports an outside peg and risks making Warby's optometry rollout sound more proven as healthcare retail than the facts support.

B misses the independent-optometry backlash angle entirely. That is probably the sharpest non-friendly story in the update, and skipping it makes the set less useful to a founder preparing for real reporters.
